html:
The forced swap of peoples between Greece and Turkey agreed at Lausanne on 30 January 1923. About 1.2 million Orthodox Christians left Anatolia and Eastern Thrace for Greece, and some 400,000 Muslims went from Greece to Turkey.

It followed the Greco-Turkish War, which ended with Greek defeat in Anatolia and the burning of Smyrna in 1922. Most Anatolian Greeks had already fled by the time the deal was signed. The convention, later part of the Treaty of Lausanne, made their exile permanent and forced out the rest. It was the first big exchange of populations in international law.

The test was religion, not language. Turkish speaking Orthodox Christians from central Anatolia were sent to Greece, and Greek speaking Muslims from Crete to Turkey. The Greeks of Istanbul and the Muslims of Western Thrace were allowed to stay.

The new Turkish Republic lost much of its merchant class. In Greece refugees made up about a fifth of the population, settled in new suburbs of Athens and Thessaloniki and across Macedonia, and brought their music and food. The European side of the story is the exchange seen from Greece.
sum: The forced swap of peoples between Greece and Turkey agreed at Lausanne on 30 January 1923. About 1.2 million Orthodox Christians left Anatolia and Eastern Thrace for Greece, and some 400,000 Muslims went from Greece to Turkey.
